title: Debounced input & autosave with timers
objectives: Write a debounce that keeps its setTimeout handle in a ref and cancels it on each keystroke
Predict the stale value a debounced save sends when it reads state instead of e.target.value
Write a blur commit that cancels the pending timer and dedupes against a lastCommitted ref
Explain why unmounting does not cancel timers, and write the empty-deps cleanup that does
Choose debounce or throttle from a requirement: once after activity stops vs capped rate during it

sources.title: React 18 Upgrade Guide (no warning about setState on unmounted components)

questions.prompt: You're debouncing an autosave inside a component. Where should the setTimeout handle be stored?

options.text: In a ref — it survives re-renders and changing it shouldn't re-render anything
In state, so React knows a save is pending
In a plain `let` at the top of the component
In a module-level variable outside the component

questions.explanation: The handle must persist between renders (so the next keystroke can cancel the previous timer) but is never displayed. That's exactly a ref. A plain `let` resets every render, so nothing gets cancelled and you save once per keystroke. State would re-render on every keystroke for a value nobody shows. A module variable persists but is shared by every instance of the component — two rename fields would cancel each other's saves.

questions.prompt: In `onChange={(e) => { setText(e.target.value); scheduleCommit(???) }}`, why must you pass `e.target.value` rather than `text`?

options.text: `text` in this handler is still the previous render's value — `setText` doesn't change the current variable
`text` is typed as `unknown` inside event handlers
Reading state inside a handler forces an extra render
It makes no difference — both are the same string

questions.explanation: State updates don't mutate the `text` const; they schedule a render that creates a new one. Inside this handler `text` is the value from the render that created the handler — one keystroke behind. Read the fresh value off the event whenever you need the value you just typed. (The functional form `setText(t => …)` doesn't help here: it fixes what goes into state, not what the timer callback reads.)

questions.prompt: What is the empty-dependency `useEffect(() => () => clearTimeout(timer.current), [])` actually protecting you from?

options.text: A pending save firing after the component is gone — committing edits for a screen the user already left
A memory leak in the timer queue that would grow forever
React rendering the component twice in StrictMode
The input showing a stale value after remount

questions.explanation: Timers outlive components. Without the cleanup, a timer scheduled a moment before unmount still fires and calls `onCommit` — a write the user didn't ask for, sometimes against a closed modal or a different record. (Since React 18, React no longer warns about setting state after unmount, and `onCommit` usually isn't a setState anyway, so this bug is silent.) One timeout is not a meaningful memory leak; the unwanted side effect is the problem.

options.text: So the already-scheduled timer can't fire afterwards and send a second, redundant save
Because clearTimeout is required before any commit, timer or not
Because clearing the timer is what returns focus to the input
Because clearTimeout flushes the pending callback synchronously

questions.explanation: Blur is an explicit "I'm done" — commit now rather than making the user wait out the delay. But a timer from the last keystroke is usually still pending; if you don't cancel it, it fires a second later and writes again. `clearTimeout` cancels, it never flushes.

questions.prompt: The requirement is "update the progress bar as the user drags, but no more than 10 times a second." Debounce or throttle?

options.text: Throttle — run at most once per interval *while* the activity continues
Debounce — run once after the activity stops
Either; they're two names for the same technique
Neither — this needs requestAnimationFrame exclusively

questions.explanation: Debounce waits for silence, so a debounced progress bar would sit frozen for the entire drag and jump at the end. Throttle emits during the activity at a capped rate — the right tool when intermediate values matter. Autosave and search-as-you-type are the debounce cases: only the final value matters.

prompts.prompt: Complete the debounce: cancel any pending timer, then schedule a new commit 1s out. Store the handle so the next keystroke can cancel it.
prompts.explanation: Every keystroke cancels the still-pending save (`clearTimeout`) and takes a new receipt (`setTimeout`), stored on `timer.current` so the next keystroke can find it. Only the keystroke not followed by another within 1s survives.

prompts.prompt: Kill any pending timer when the component unmounts — an effect that returns only a cleanup function and never re-runs.
prompts.explanation: The effect body immediately *returns* another arrow function — that returned function is the cleanup. With `[]` deps the effect never re-runs, so the cleanup runs exactly once: at unmount.

prompts.prompt: Commit without ever saving the same value twice. Fill in the dedupe guard and the ref it compares against.
prompts.explanation: Both paths — the timer firing and the blur handler — go through `commit`, so the "have we already saved this?" question is asked in exactly one place. The baseline is `lastCommitted`, not the `title` prop: after a save the prop may not have caught up (so comparing to it saves the same text twice), and typing the original title back after a save would never be saved at all.

code: // The user types "hello" (5 keystrokes) quickly, then waits.
snippets.question: How many times is onCommit called?
snippets.explanation: `let timer` is re-created on every render, so each keystroke's `clearTimeout(timer)` clears `undefined` — a no-op — and every scheduled save survives. Five timers fire ~1s later: five saves. The whole point of the ref is that `timer.current` is the *same box* across renders, so the next keystroke can actually find and cancel the previous timer.

code: // The user types "hello" quickly and stops.
snippets.question: What string does onCommit finally receive?
snippets.explanation: The surviving timer is the one scheduled by the last keystroke — but that handler closed over the `text` from the render *before* it, which was "hell". The state update to "hello" hasn't rendered yet when `schedule()` runs. Passing `e.target.value` explicitly is what makes the committed value the value on screen.

code: // No cleanup effect. The user types one character into the rename field,
// then immediately closes the modal (the component unmounts) 200ms later.
snippets.question: Does onCommit run, and when?
acceptable: yes, 1s after the keystroke even though the component is gone
snippets.explanation: Unmounting a component does not cancel its timers — the callback is queued on the platform, not on React. It fires ~800ms after the modal closes and commits an edit the user abandoned. React doesn't warn about it (there's no setState involved, and since React 18 React doesn't warn about setState after unmount either), so the only defense is the cleanup that calls `clearTimeout` on unmount.
